name: Kulazngi / Kulaz, also Kulisi Agaw
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Yaregal Allene Teferra. 2016. A Grammar of Kulazngi. PhD dissertation, Addis Ababa University (supervisor Zelealem Leyew). Open download, AAU ETD hdl 12345678/16310. Secondary: Zelealem Leyew. n.d. [c. 2012; fieldwork Jan 2010]. The Kulisi Agaw: The People and their Language. Report to the Gesellschaft fuer bedrohte Sprachen, Addis Ababa University, 78 pp.
catalog_locator: Ch. 2, sec. 2.3.1 'Is Kulazngi a tone language?', pp. 43-44 and sec. 2.3.2 'Toneme Inventory', p. 45. Leyew report: sec. 2.1.4 'Tone', pp. 12-13.
catalog_quote: By all definitions above, Kulazngi is a tone language, or it is not a mere pitch-accent language, because every syllable in a word bears low, mid, or high tone having a lexical as well as a grammatical function. A significant number of lexical items of the same word class show meaning variation due to pitch variation only. Pitch also plays a role to express grammatical distinction. ... In Kulazngi, the tone carried in a syllable may be an essential feature in determining the meaning or the grammatical feature of the word. For example, ... bér (H) 'gate', múrí (H.H) 'snake', and mùrí (L.H) 'village'. Hence, Kulazngi is a tone language with the above three tone levels (high, low, mid) plus a falling tone both at a lexical and a morphological level [p. 44] ... Among the Agaw languages, Bilin and Awngi are reported to be tone languages while Kemanteney has only stress (Hetzron, 1976: 2). ... the present study reveals that every syllable of Kulazngi words carries a relative pitch accent among which some are contrastive, which distinguish between various lexical and grammatical forms, which is a feature that places a language at tonal position. ... In this study, Kulazngi has three level (high, low, mid) and one contour (HL) tones. Each level tone can appear with monosyllabic and disyllabic words. While high and low tones have no positional restriction, mid tone never occurs word initially in polysyllabic words; it does not occur sequentially (as M.M) either. [p. 45]
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kunfäl/Kulazngi is described as a lexical and grammatical tone language (H, M, L, HL) in which every syllable carries a tone; the grammar gives no rule for word stress and never says where stress falls. The earlier sketch by Zelealem Leyew (n.d., pp.12-13) says it cannot yet be determined whether Kulisi is a pitch accent or a tone language and whether its pitch distinctions are 'distinct from stress or pitch accent'; Yaregal 2016 resolves this in favour of tone.
new_statements.exceptions: None about stress. Tonal distribution restrictions only: mid tone not word-initial in polysyllables and never in M.M sequences; HL contour restricted to mono- and disyllabic nouns; minimal pairs e.g. múrí (H.H) 'snake' vs mùrí (L.H) 'village'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (nouns, adjectives, verbs in citation form); data from the Bagʷsa dialect of Kulazngi in Jawi wereda. No statement on phrase-level prominence.
new_statements.identity_note: kunf1238 'Kunfal' is a Glottolog Bookkeeping code: ISO 639-3 xuf was retired on 2008-01-14 (change request 2007-044) and merged into awn Awngi after the 2005 SIL survey found the K'wara/Alefa/Jawi lowland Agaw to be a dialect of Awngi (72-74 % lexical similarity, one-sided intelligibility). The speakers reject 'Kunfäl' (pejorative Amharic exonym); they call themselves Kulisi Agaw (Zelealem Leyew) or Kulaz / Kulazngi (Yaregal 2016), and the older shifted-from language is Kumpalngi. The deciding source (Yaregal 2016) describes the Bagʷsa dialect of Kulazngi in Jawi wereda, Awi Zone. The parent language Awngi (awng1244) is already in the catalog coded 'conflict' (Hetzron penult stress vs Joswig 2010 'no evidence' vs Worku 1986 initial/final); the Kulazngi statement is tone-only and belongs under awng1244 as a dialect record unless the catalog counts Kunfäl as a separate entity — by our rule that each source is filed under the language's current Glottolog code (a retired code does not make a separate language) a retired code does not make a separate language, so the catalog gate should decide whether this is a new row or an addition to awng1244.

sources.note: Kulazngi (= Kunfäl) is a tone language with three level tones (H, M, L) plus a HL contour, every syllable bearing a tone with lexical and grammatical function (pp. 44-45); the only occurrence of the word 'stress' in the whole thesis is the remark that Kemanteney 'has only stress' (Hetzron 1976), so it is silent on word stress in Kulazngi itself.

sources.citation: Joswig, Andreas & Hussein Mohammed. 2011. A Sociolinguistic Survey Report; Revisiting the Southern Agaw Language Areas of Ethiopia. SIL Electronic Survey Report 2011-047. Dallas: SIL International, 26 pp.
sources.note: Survey report (intelligibility tests, 72-74% lexical similarity of the K'wara/Aswäl Agaw variety with Awngi dialects, recommended as a dialect of Awngi). Wordlist sec. 6.2 p.14: 'The marking of tone is not based on careful analysis but on first hearing only and is, therefore, not reliable.' Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Zelealem Leyew. n.d. [c. 2011-2012; fieldwork January 2010]. The Kulisi Agaw: The People and their Language. Report to the Gesellschaft für bedrohte Sprachen, Dept. of Linguistics, Addis Ababa University, 78 pp. Sec. 2.1.4 'Tone', pp. 12-13.
sources.note: p.12: 'Whether they are grammatical or lexical or both and whether or not they are distinct from stress or pitch accent still needs further description.' Gives four tonal minimal pairs (yíwi 'wrist' / yiwí 'mine', múri 'village' / murí 'snake', etc.) and concludes p.13: 'at this point, it is difficult to determine whether Kulisi is a pitch accent or a tone language.' No word-stress rule.
